# 1.1 Foundations of Geography

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The five themes

Geography organises itself around five recurring questions:

| Theme | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Location** | Where something is — absolute (coordinates) or relative (in relation to other places) |
| **Place** | The human and physical characteristics of a location |
| **Region** | An area with **uniform physical or human characteristics** |
| **Movement** | Communication, migration, and diffusion across Earth's surface |
| **Human-Environment Interaction (HEI)** | Interactions between humans and the Earth |

**Spatial analysis** — synthesising topics from different fields — is what holds these together. Geography as a whole depends on it: the discipline is defined less by *what* it studies than by the fact that it asks **where**, and why there.

**Physical geography** is the spatial analysis of physical elements, processes, and systems.

## Systems thinking

A **system** is a set of ordered, interrelated components and their attributes.

An **open system** has **inputs and outputs flowing in and out**. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings.

Earth is effectively a **closed system for matter** — apart from meteorites, no new material arrives — but an **open system for energy**, receiving solar radiation and re-radiating heat. That distinction underlies almost every environmental argument in the course: matter is finite and must cycle, energy flows through.

## The spheres

| Sphere | Contents |
|---|---|
| **Atmosphere** | Gases surrounding the Earth |
| **Hydrosphere** | All the Earth's water |
| **Cryosphere** | The **frozen portion of the hydrosphere** |
| **Lithosphere** | Earth's crust and the upper portion of the mantle beneath it |
| **Biosphere (ecosphere)** | The area in which physical and chemical factors form the context of **life** |

The **biosphere overlaps with all the others**, extending from the seafloor upward — which is why almost no environmental question stays within one sphere.

## The scientific method

Simple, organised steps leading toward concrete, objective conclusions:

$$\text{observation} \rightarrow \text{hypothesis and predictions} \rightarrow \text{experiment and measurement} \rightarrow \text{peer review}$$

## The shape of the Earth

**Geodesy** is the science that determines Earth's shape and size through surveys and calculations. The **geoid** is the resulting shape of the Earth — not a perfect sphere but slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator.

**Sphericity** — Earth's roughly spherical shape — has a consequence that recurs throughout physical geography: it causes **the parallel rays of the sun to strike Earth's surface at uneven angles**. The same beam of sunlight is spread over a larger area near the poles than at the equator, so **insolation angles and net radiation vary with latitude**. This is why **insolation angles and net radiation vary with latitude**, and it is the geometry behind the seasons.

## The coordinate grid

**Latitude** is angular distance north or south of the equator. A **parallel** is a line connecting all points at the same latitude.

**Longitude** is angular distance east or west of the **Prime Meridian**, at **0°**, which passes through **Greenwich**.

**Great circle:** any circle around the Earth whose plane passes through the **centre** of the Earth — the equator and every full meridian circle. Each meridian is half of a great circle. Great circles give the shortest distance between two points on a sphere, which is why long-haul flight paths look curved on a flat map.

**Small circle:** also a circle on the Earth's surface, but one whose plane does **not** pass through the centre — every parallel except the equator.

## Time

**GMT (Greenwich Mean Time)** was the official standard mean time. **UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)** is the modern standard. **Mean solar time** divides the day into 24 hours.

## Key latitudes

| Line | Latitude | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| **Tropic of Cancer** | 23.5°N | Northern limit of the subsolar point |
| **Tropic of Capricorn** | 23.5°S | Southern limit of the subsolar point |
| **Arctic Circle** | 66.5°N | Lowest northern latitude with 24-hour daylight or darkness |
| **Antarctic Circle** | 66.5°S | Lowest southern latitude with 24-hour daylight or darkness |

Both pairs of numbers come from the same source: Earth's **23.5° axial tilt**. The tropics are at 23.5°, and the polar circles at 90° − 23.5° = 66.5°.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Location** | Where something is — absolute (coordinates) or relative (in relation to other places) |
| **Place** | The human and physical characteristics of a location |
| **Region** | An area with uniform physical or human characteristics |
| **Movement** | Communication, migration, and diffusion across Earth's surface |
| **Human-Environment Interaction (HEI)** | Interactions between humans and the Earth |
| **Spatial analysis** | Synthesising topics from different fields |
| **Physical geography** | The spatial analysis of physical elements, processes, and systems |
| **System** | A set of ordered, interrelated components and their attributes |
| **Open system** | A system with inputs and outputs flowing in and out |
| **Closed system** | A system that exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings |
| **Atmosphere** | Gases surrounding the Earth |
| **Hydrosphere** | All the Earth's water |
| **Cryosphere** | The frozen portion of the hydrosphere |
| **Lithosphere** | Earth's crust and the upper portion of the mantle beneath it |
| **Biosphere (ecosphere)** | The area in which physical and chemical factors form the context of life |
| **Scientific method** | Simple, organised steps leading toward concrete, objective conclusions: observation, hypothesis and predictions, experiment and measurement, peer review |
| **Geodesy** | The science that determines Earth's shape and size through surveys and calculations |
| **Geoid** | The resulting shape of the Earth — not a perfect sphere but slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator |
| **Sphericity** | Earth's roughly spherical shape, which causes the parallel rays of the sun to strike Earth's surface at uneven angles |
| **Latitude** | Angular distance north or south of the equator |
| **Parallel** | A line connecting all points at the same latitude |
| **Longitude** | Angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian |
| **Prime Meridian** | The meridian at 0°, which passes through Greenwich |
| **Great circle** | Any circle around the Earth whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth |
| **Small circle** | A circle on the Earth's surface whose plane does not pass through the centre |
| **GMT (Greenwich Mean Time)** | The official standard mean time |
| **UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)** | The modern standard time |
| **Mean solar time** | Time that divides the day into 24 hours |
| **Tropic of Cancer** | 23.5°N — the northern limit of the subsolar point |
| **Tropic of Capricorn** | 23.5°S — the southern limit of the subsolar point |
| **Arctic Circle** | 66.5°N — the lowest northern latitude with 24-hour daylight or darkness |
| **Antarctic Circle** | 66.5°S — the lowest southern latitude with 24-hour daylight or darkness |

# 1.2 Maps and Geospatial Technology

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Cartography** is the science of mapmaking.

## Scale

**Scale** relates the size of a unit on the map to the size of the same unit on the ground. Three ways of expressing it:

| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| **Fraction (representative fraction)** | 1:100, or 1/100 |
| **Written** | 1 cm = 1 m |
| **Graphic** | A drawn bar: \|---1---2---3\| m |

**The larger the denominator, the smaller the scale**, and vice versa. A 1:1,000,000 map is small-scale (little detail, large area); a 1:1,000 map is large-scale (much detail, small area). This is the reverse of what the words suggest, and is the most common error in the topic.

**The graphic scale is the only one that survives reproduction**: it scales with the map when the map is enlarged or reduced, so it is always right, while a written or fractional scale becomes wrong the moment the map is photocopied at a different size.

## Map projections

A **map projection** is the translation of the Earth onto a flat surface. **Every projection has distortion** — distance, direction, area, shape, or proximity.

This is not a failure of cartographers but a mathematical necessity: a sphere cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing. The only question is **which property you choose to preserve**.

Two properties a projection may preserve:

- **Equal area (equivalence)** — preserves **area**
- **True shape (conformality)** — preserves **shape**

**Both of these distort one property while preserving the other.** No projection does both.

### Types

**Cylindrical** — for example the **Mercator**, which **preserves shape but distorts area**, increasingly so toward the poles. It may be **normal** (east-west), **transverse** (north-south), or **oblique** (angled). Mercator is used for **navigation** because **rhumb lines** — lines of constant compass bearing — are straight on it. That single property made it indispensable to sailors and is the reason a projection that makes Greenland look the size of Africa remained in universal use.

**Planar (gnomonic, azimuthal)** — shows **great circle routes as straight lines**, which is useful for aviation and radio, but produces **a great deal of distortion in both shape and area**.

**Standard line:** the line on a projection where there is **zero distortion**. Distortion increases with distance from it.

## Geospatial technology

**GPS (Global Positioning System)** gives your **absolute location**. It requires **at least four satellites — three for position and one for time** — and returns latitude, longitude, and elevation.

Note the split the guide draws: **three satellites fix the position, and the fourth supplies the time**.

**Remote sensing** is obtaining information about distant objects **without physical contact**.

- **Passive remote sensing** records wavelengths **present naturally** — ordinary aerial photography records reflected sunlight
- **Active remote sensing** **emits its own waves** and records those returned; the returned rays are called **backscatter**. **LiDAR** is an active system used for terrain mapping

The practical difference: passive systems cannot work at night or through cloud, active systems can.

**Photogrammetry** is obtaining measurements from photographs.

**GIS (Geographic Information System)** is a computer-based tool for gathering, manipulating, and analysing geographic information. Data are arranged in **layers**, each holding one kind of information — elevation, roads, population, land use — which can be overlaid and analysed together.

The layer model is what makes GIS powerful: questions that would be impossible to answer from any single map ("which schools are within a flood zone and more than 5 km from a hospital?") become straightforward when the relevant layers can be combined.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cartography** | The science of mapmaking |
| **Scale** | The relation of the size of a unit on the map to the size of the same unit on the ground |
| **Representative fraction** | Scale expressed as a fraction, for example 1:100 or 1/100 |
| **Graphic scale** | Scale expressed as a drawn bar; the only form that survives reproduction, since it enlarges and reduces with the map |
| **Map projection** | The translation of the Earth onto a flat surface; every projection has distortion |
| **Equal area (equivalence)** | A projection property that preserves area |
| **True shape (conformality)** | A projection property that preserves shape |
| **Cylindrical projection** | A projection class including the Mercator; may be normal (east-west), transverse (north-south), or oblique (angled) |
| **Mercator** | A cylindrical projection that preserves shape but distorts area, increasingly so toward the poles; used for navigation |
| **Rhumb line** | A line of constant compass bearing, which is straight on the Mercator projection |
| **Planar (gnomonic, azimuthal) projection** | A projection showing great circle routes as straight lines, but producing a great deal of distortion in both shape and area |
| **Standard line** | The line on a projection where there is zero distortion; distortion increases with distance from it |
| **GPS (Global Positioning System)** | A system giving absolute location; requires at least four satellites — three for position and one for time — and returns latitude, longitude, and elevation |
| **Remote sensing** | Obtaining information about distant objects without physical contact |
| **Passive remote sensing** | Remote sensing that records wavelengths present naturally, as in ordinary aerial photography |
| **Active remote sensing** | Remote sensing that emits its own waves and records those returned |
| **Backscatter** | The returned rays recorded by an active remote sensing system |
| **LiDAR** | An active remote sensing system used for terrain mapping |
| **Photogrammetry** | Obtaining measurements from photographs |
| **GIS (Geographic Information System)** | A computer-based tool for gathering, manipulating, and analysing geographic information, with data arranged in layers that can be overlaid |

# 2.1 The Sun and Solar Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The structure of the Sun

| Layer | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Photosphere** | The visible surface |
| **Chromosphere** | Cannot normally be observed |
| **Corona** | The outer atmosphere; visible to the naked eye **only during a total solar eclipse**, or with a coronagraph |

## Fusion

**Fusion** is two or more atomic nuclei combining to form one or more new nuclei. In the Sun it **releases far more energy than fission**, converting **mass into energy**.

## Solar activity

**The solar cycle** is the periodic variation in the Sun's activity and appearance over time, running on an approximately **11-year** cycle.

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **Sunspot** | A surface disturbance caused by a magnetic storm; a **cooler** area |
| **Faculae** | Bright spots near sunspots |
| **Solar minimum** | Years when fewer sunspots are visible |
| **Solar maximum** | Years when sunspots are most numerous |
| **Solar flare** | A **violent eruption of plasma**; lasts minutes to hours; harmful |
| **Prominence** | A **large, bright gaseous loop** arcing from the surface; contains much **cooler** plasma than a flare; lasts for months; relatively harmless |

Note the contrast between flares and prominences: both are eruptions, but one is short, violent, and dangerous, the other long-lived and largely benign.

**Solar wind** consists of clouds of electrically charged particles emitted from the Sun. It takes about **three days** to reach Earth and **disrupts radio broadcasts and satellite transmissions**.

**Coronal mass ejections (CMEs)** are large outbursts of charged material, and are what cause **auroras** — folded sheets of green, yellow, blue, and red light that appear at **high latitudes**.

## The magnetosphere

The **magnetosphere** is the magnetic field generated by dynamo-like motions inside our planet. It **deflects the solar wind toward Earth's poles**, so that only a small portion enters the upper atmosphere.

Both facts about auroras follow from this: they appear at high latitudes because that is where the magnetosphere funnels the particles, and the atmosphere would be steadily stripped away without that deflection. The aurora is the visible edge of Earth's radiation shield working.

## Radiation

The **electromagnetic spectrum** is the range of all possible wavelengths of electromagnetic energy.

- **Wavelength** — the distance between corresponding points on two successive waves. **The hotter the object, the shorter the wavelengths it emits.**
- **Frequency** — the number of waves passing a fixed point each second.

Because the Sun is far hotter than the Earth, the Sun emits **ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma, visible, and infrared** radiation — **shortwave** radiation overall — while the Earth emits mostly **longwave infrared**.

That asymmetry is the entire basis of the greenhouse effect: the atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming shortwave radiation and largely opaque to outgoing longwave radiation.

A **blackbody** is a perfect absorber of radiant energy, which also emits all the radiant energy it receives.

## Insolation

**Insolation** is **incoming solar radiation intercepted by the Earth**.

The **thermopause** is the outer boundary of Earth's energy system, at the top of the atmosphere.

The **solar constant** is the average insolation received at the thermopause when Earth is at its average distance from the Sun: **1372 W/m²**.

The **subsolar point** is the point where insolation arrives **perpendicular to the surface**. It lies between **23.5°N and 23.5°S**, which is why **equatorial regions receive far more insolation than polar regions** — the sphericity argument from 1.1, stated quantitatively.

## Earth's orbit

**Aphelion** is Earth's farthest position from the Sun; **perihelion** the nearest. Earth's orbit changes over long periods, but these variations have little effect on ordinary seasonal patterns.

This is worth stating plainly because it corrects the most persistent misconception in the subject: **the seasons are not caused by distance from the Sun.** Earth is actually closest to the Sun during the northern winter. The cause is axial tilt (2.2).

## Solar eclipses

| Type | Observed from |
|---|---|
| **Full (total) eclipse** | The **umbra** |
| **Annular eclipse** | The **antumbra** |
| **Partial eclipse** | The **penumbra** |

On average there are about **2.38 solar eclipses each year**, with a **total** solar eclipse roughly once every **1.5 years** — but visible from any given location only very rarely, since the umbra traces a narrow path across the surface.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Photosphere** | The visible surface of the Sun |
| **Chromosphere** | The layer of the Sun that cannot normally be observed |
| **Corona** | The Sun's outer atmosphere; visible to the naked eye only during a total solar eclipse, or with a coronagraph |
| **Fusion** | Two or more atomic nuclei combining to form one or more new nuclei, converting mass into energy and releasing far more energy than fission |
| **The solar cycle** | The periodic variation in the Sun's activity and appearance over time, running on an approximately 11-year cycle |
| **Sunspot** | A surface disturbance caused by a magnetic storm; a cooler area |
| **Faculae** | Bright spots near sunspots |
| **Solar minimum** | Years when fewer sunspots are visible |
| **Solar maximum** | Years when sunspots are most numerous |
| **Solar flare** | A violent eruption of plasma; lasts minutes to hours; harmful |
| **Prominence** | A large, bright gaseous loop arcing from the surface, containing much cooler plasma than a flare; lasts for months and is relatively harmless |
| **Solar wind** | Clouds of electrically charged particles emitted from the Sun; takes about three days to reach Earth and disrupts radio broadcasts and satellite transmissions |
| **Coronal mass ejection (CME)** | A large outburst of charged material from the Sun |
| **Aurora** | Folded sheets of green, yellow, blue, and red light appearing at high latitudes, caused by coronal mass ejections |
| **Magnetosphere** | The magnetic field generated by dynamo-like motions inside our planet, which deflects the solar wind toward Earth's poles |
| **Electromagnetic spectrum** | The range of all possible wavelengths of electromagnetic energy |
| **Wavelength** | The distance between corresponding points on two successive waves; the hotter the object, the shorter the wavelengths it emits |
| **Frequency** | The number of waves passing a fixed point each second |
| **Blackbody** | A perfect absorber of radiant energy, which also emits all the radiant energy it receives |
| **Insolation** | Incoming solar radiation intercepted by the Earth |
| **Thermopause** | The outer boundary of Earth's energy system, at the top of the atmosphere |
| **Solar constant** | The average insolation received at the thermopause when Earth is at its average distance from the Sun: 1372 W/m² |
| **Subsolar point** | The point where insolation arrives perpendicular to the surface; it lies between 23.5°N and 23.5°S |
| **Aphelion** | Earth's farthest position from the Sun |
| **Perihelion** | Earth's nearest position to the Sun |
| **Full (total) eclipse** | A solar eclipse observed from the umbra |
| **Annular eclipse** | A solar eclipse observed from the antumbra |
| **Partial eclipse** | A solar eclipse observed from the penumbra |

# 2.2 Earth–Sun Relations and the Seasons

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The five causes of seasons

Seasons are caused by variations in **altitude** (of the Sun), **declination** (of the subsolar point), and **daylength**. These are in turn caused by five properties of Earth's motion:

| Cause | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Revolution** | Earth's orbit around the Sun |
| **Rotation** | Earth's turning on its axis |
| **Axial tilt** | The 23.5° tilt of the axis relative to the plane of the ecliptic |
| **Axial parallelism** | Earth's axis maintains the **same alignment** throughout the orbit |
| **Sphericity** | Earth's spherical shape |

**Axial parallelism** is the cause most often left out and the one that makes the whole system work. Because the axis keeps pointing the same way in space all year, the northern hemisphere tilts *toward* the Sun in June and *away* in December. If the axis swivelled to keep pointing at the Sun, there would be no seasons at all.

The **axis** is an imaginary line extending through the planet from geographic North to South pole. The **plane of the ecliptic** is the plane containing Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun.

## Daylength

**Sunrise** is the moment when the Sun first appears; **sunset** the moment it entirely disappears.

**Daylength never changes on the equator** — 12 hours of day, 12 of night, all year — and **varies more the more extreme the latitude**, with the poles experiencing six months of daylight and six of darkness.

The **circle of illumination** is the dividing line between day and night.

**Twilight** is the period of diffused light around the edges of the day: **dawn** before sunrise, **dusk** after sunset.

## The solstices and equinoxes

| Event | Subsolar point | Circle of illumination |
|---|---|---|
| **June solstice** | 23.5°N (Tropic of Cancer) | Excludes the South Pole; North Pole in continuous daylight |
| **September equinox** | 0° (equator) | Passes through both poles; day and night equal everywhere |
| **December solstice** | 23.5°S (Tropic of Capricorn) | **Excludes the North Pole**; South Pole in continuous daylight |
| **March equinox** | 0° (equator) | Passes through both poles |

Note the naming trap: the **December solstice** is the **winter** solstice in the Northern Hemisphere but the **summer** solstice in the Southern; the **March equinox** is the **vernal** equinox in the north and the **autumnal** equinox in the south. Using "June solstice" and "December solstice" avoids the ambiguity entirely, which is why the modern convention prefers them.

The subsolar point migrates between the two tropics over the year — reaching **23.5°N at the June solstice** and **23.5°S at the December solstice** — which is precisely why those latitudes are defined where they are.

## Finding your latitude

**From the position of the Sun.** With $x$ = latitude, $A$ = solar altitude (the Sun's height above the horizon at local noon), and $B$ = solar declination (the latitude of the subsolar point):

- If you are in the Northern Hemisphere and the **subsolar point is also in the Northern Hemisphere**:
  $$x = (90 - A) + |B|$$
- If you are in the Northern Hemisphere and the **subsolar point is in the Southern Hemisphere**:
  $$x = (90 - A) - |B|$$

The sign depends on whether the subsolar point is on your side of the equator, which is the only thing to get right. Be able to **graph this relationship** as well as calculate it.

**From the North Star.** Measure the angle of Polaris above the horizon; **that angle equals your latitude**. This works only in the Northern Hemisphere, since Polaris sits almost directly above the North Pole — from the pole it is overhead (90°), and from the equator it sits on the horizon (0°).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Revolution** | Earth's orbit around the Sun |
| **Rotation** | Earth's turning on its axis |
| **Axial tilt** | The 23.5° tilt of the axis relative to the plane of the ecliptic |
| **Axial parallelism** | The fact that Earth's axis maintains the same alignment throughout the orbit |
| **Sphericity** | Earth's spherical shape |
| **Axis** | An imaginary line extending through the planet from geographic North to South pole |
| **Plane of the ecliptic** | The plane containing Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun |
| **Sunrise** | The moment when the Sun first appears |
| **Sunset** | The moment the Sun entirely disappears |
| **Circle of illumination** | The dividing line between day and night |
| **Twilight** | The period of diffused light around the edges of the day |
| **Dawn** | Twilight before sunrise |
| **Dusk** | Twilight after sunset |
| **June solstice** | The event when the subsolar point reaches 23.5°N (Tropic of Cancer); the circle of illumination excludes the South Pole and the North Pole is in continuous daylight |
| **December solstice** | The event when the subsolar point reaches 23.5°S (Tropic of Capricorn); the circle of illumination excludes the North Pole and the South Pole is in continuous daylight |
| **September equinox** | The event when the subsolar point is at 0° (the equator); the circle of illumination passes through both poles and day and night are equal everywhere |
| **March equinox** | The event when the subsolar point is at 0° (the equator); the circle of illumination passes through both poles. The vernal equinox in the north and the autumnal equinox in the south |
| **Solar altitude** | The Sun's height above the horizon at local noon |
| **Solar declination** | The latitude of the subsolar point |

# 3.1 The Hydrologic Cycle and the Water Budget

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Where water goes when it lands

| Process | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Precipitation** | Moisture supply to Earth's surface |
| **Infiltration** | Water soaking into the soil |
| **Overland flow / surface runoff** | Water that does **not** soak in and moves downhill |
| **Streamflow** | When overland flow begins to move in channels |
| **Percolation** | Water that has already infiltrated moving **downwards** through the soil |
| **Base flow** | Where the **water table intersects a stream channel**, feeding the stream from below |

The split between infiltration and overland flow is the key fork in the whole system. Water that infiltrates recharges soil moisture and groundwater; water that runs off produces streamflow and erosion. Anything that reduces infiltration — paving, compaction, saturated ground — increases flooding downstream.

## Soil moisture

The **soil moisture zone** is the volume of subsurface water stored in the soil that is **accessible to plant roots**.

Not all soil water is available to plants:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Hygroscopic water** | **Inaccessible** to plants; held too tightly to soil particles. Exists in all climates |
| **Capillary water** | **Accessible** to plants; held in the soil by **surface tension** |
| **Gravitational water** | Surplus water in the soil body after the soil becomes **saturated**; drains away under gravity |
| **Field capacity** | The **storage capacity** — the maximum water a given soil can hold that is available to plants |
| **Wilting point** | When only inaccessible water remains; **plants die** |

**Porosity** is the available pore space in a soil. **Permeability** is the property that determines the **rate of recharge** — how fast water can move through.

Porosity and permeability are not the same thing, and clay demonstrates why: clay is highly porous but nearly impermeable, because the pores are tiny and poorly connected. A soil can hold a great deal of water and still transmit it very slowly.

**Soil moisture utilisation** is plants' usage of available soil moisture. **Soil moisture recharge** is when infiltrating water replenishes it.

## Evapotranspiration

**Potential evapotranspiration (POTET)** is the amount of water that **would** evaporate and transpire **given optimum moisture conditions** — a measure of atmospheric demand.

**Actual evapotranspiration (ACTET)** is potential evapotranspiration **minus the deficit** — the amount actually lost.

$$\text{ACTET} = \text{POTET} - \text{deficit}$$

The gap between the two is the whole point of the water budget: potential says what the atmosphere *wants*, actual says what the ground can *supply*.

## The water budget

The **water budget** is derived from **precipitation and soil moisture, minus evapotranspiration**.

- **Surplus** — extra water remaining after expenditure demands are met
- **Deficit** — when precipitation and soil moisture are **insufficient** to meet demands

## Drought

Four kinds, defined by what is affected rather than by rainfall alone:

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Meteorological** | Defined by the degree of dryness compared to the **regional average** — region-specific |
| **Agricultural** | When shortages of precipitation and soil moisture **affect crop yields** |
| **Hydrological** | The effect of precipitation shortages on **water supply** |
| **Socioeconomic** | When reduced water supply causes **demand for goods and services to exceed it** |

Two features of this classification are worth noting. First, drought is **relative**: 200 mm of rain is a wet year in a desert and a catastrophe in Britain, which is why meteorological drought is defined against the regional average. Second, the four types occur in **sequence** — meteorological drought comes first, and the others follow with a lag as reservoirs, soils, and economies work through their reserves.

## Related terms

**Hydropower** is electricity generated using the power of moving water.

A **wetland** is an area permanently or seasonally saturated with water — the transitional environment where the water table meets or exceeds the surface.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Precipitation** | Moisture supply to Earth's surface |
| **Infiltration** | Water soaking into the soil |
| **Overland flow / surface runoff** | Water that does not soak in and moves downhill |
| **Streamflow** | When overland flow begins to move in channels |
| **Percolation** | Water that has already infiltrated moving downwards through the soil |
| **Base flow** | Where the water table intersects a stream channel, feeding the stream from below |
| **Soil moisture zone** | The volume of subsurface water stored in the soil that is accessible to plant roots |
| **Hygroscopic water** | Soil water inaccessible to plants, held too tightly to soil particles; exists in all climates |
| **Capillary water** | Soil water accessible to plants, held in the soil by surface tension |
| **Gravitational water** | Surplus water in the soil body after the soil becomes saturated; drains away under gravity |
| **Field capacity** | The storage capacity — the maximum water a given soil can hold that is available to plants |
| **Wilting point** | When only inaccessible water remains and plants die |
| **Porosity** | The available pore space in a soil |
| **Permeability** | The property that determines the rate of recharge — how fast water can move through |
| **Soil moisture utilisation** | Plants' usage of available soil moisture |
| **Soil moisture recharge** | When infiltrating water replenishes soil moisture |
| **Potential evapotranspiration (POTET)** | The amount of water that would evaporate and transpire given optimum moisture conditions |
| **Actual evapotranspiration (ACTET)** | Potential evapotranspiration minus the deficit — the amount actually lost |
| **Water budget** | The balance derived from precipitation and soil moisture, minus evapotranspiration |
| **Surplus** | Extra water remaining after expenditure demands are met |
| **Deficit** | When precipitation and soil moisture are insufficient to meet demands |
| **Meteorological drought** | Drought defined by the degree of dryness compared to the regional average |
| **Agricultural drought** | When shortages of precipitation and soil moisture affect crop yields |
| **Hydrological drought** | The effect of precipitation shortages on water supply |
| **Socioeconomic drought** | When reduced water supply causes demand for goods and services to exceed it |
| **Hydropower** | Electricity generated using the power of moving water |
| **Wetland** | An area permanently or seasonally saturated with water |

# 3.2 Groundwater

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The subsurface zones

**Groundwater** is water below the surface.

| Zone | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Zone of aeration** | Soil and rock are **less than saturated** — pore spaces hold both air and water |
| **Zone of saturation** | Soil and rock are **completely saturated** |
| **Water table** | The **transition** between the two zones |

## Aquifers

An **aquifer** is a subsurface layer of **permeable** rock or unconsolidated material — silt, sand, or gravel — through which groundwater can flow **in amounts adequate for wells and springs**.

An **aquiclude** is the **impermeable** layer of rock below the groundwater.

| Type | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Unconfined aquifer** | **Permeable** layer above, **impermeable** layer below |
| **Confined aquifer** | **Impermeable** layers both above and below |

The **potentiometric surface** is the pressure level created by the pressure on the water in a **confined** aquifer — the level to which the water would rise if given the chance.

## Wells

| Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary well** | Drilled into an **unconfined** aquifer; the water is not under pressure and must be **pumped** up |
| **Artesian well** | Drilled into a **confined** aquifer; the water **rises** to the potentiometric surface |
| **Gushing artesian well** | An artesian well whose top is **lower than the potentiometric surface**, so the water rises out of the well on its own |

The distinction rests entirely on confinement. A confined aquifer is sealed above and below, so water entering at a higher elevation puts the whole body under pressure — which is why an artesian well flows without pumping.

## Overuse

**Drawdown** is the lowering of the water table of an unconfined aquifer, occurring when **the rate of pumping exceeds the rate at which the aquifer can replenish itself**.

The lowered water table around the well forms a **cone of depression** — a funnel-shaped dip centred on the well. Where many wells draw on the same aquifer, their cones overlap and the whole water table falls, which is why groundwater depletion is a collective problem that no single user can solve.

## Use

**Water withdrawal (non-consumptive use)** is the removal or diversion of water from surface or groundwater supplies **followed by the return of that water to the same supply** — as in cooling water for power stations.

**Consumptive use** is the **permanent removal** of water from the immediate environment; the water is **not returned** and is therefore not available for a second or third use. Irrigation is the largest example, since most of the water evaporates or is transpired.

The distinction matters for policy: a region can withdraw far more water than it has, provided most of the withdrawal is returned. Consumptive use is what actually depletes a supply.

## Groundwater contamination

Groundwater is difficult to clean once polluted, because it moves slowly and is inaccessible. Sources of contamination include:

**Natural sources.** Some substances found naturally in rocks or soils — **arsenic, chlorides, iron** — can dissolve into groundwater.

**Septic systems.** Outflow from septic tanks, cesspools, and privies. Their **large number and widespread use** make them a serious threat.

**Improper disposal of hazardous waste.** Many chemicals should never enter household septic systems.

**Releases and spills from stored chemicals and petroleum.** Storage tanks leak through **age and corrosion**; an underground tank leak releases its contents directly into the subsurface.

**Landfills.** Chemicals **leach** into the ground with precipitation.

**Surface impoundments.** Shallow ponds or lagoons storing and treating liquid wastes. They are required to have **liners**, but liners sometimes leak.

**Sewers and pipelines.** Sewer pipes leak into surrounding soil; pipelines carrying industrial chemicals and oil brine can too.

**Pesticides and fertilisers.** These can contaminate groundwater following **normal, registered use** — the point being that misuse is not required.

**Drainage wells**, used to drain wet areas into deeper soils, may carry agricultural chemicals and bacteria. **Injection wells and floor drains** collect stormwater, spilled liquids, and wastes.

**Improperly constructed wells** allow contaminated surface or ground water into the well. **Improperly abandoned wells** let contaminants reach the aquifer through corroded or removed casing, and are sometimes used for waste disposal. **Active drinking-water supply wells** with faulty casings or inadequate covers admit outside water. **Poorly constructed irrigation wells** are especially exposed, since pesticides and fertilisers are used in their immediate vicinity.

**Mining activities.** Precipitation leaches soluble minerals from mine wastes into the groundwater below, and pumping mines dry alters local groundwater flow.

Note how many of these are **routine rather than accidental** — normal fertiliser use, ordinary septic systems, standard landfills. Groundwater protection is therefore mostly a matter of design and regulation rather than of preventing disasters.

**Effects of contamination:** poor drinking-water quality, loss of water supply, degraded surface water systems, and **high cleanup costs**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Groundwater** | Water below the surface |
| **Zone of aeration** | The zone where soil and rock are less than saturated, pore spaces holding both air and water |
| **Zone of saturation** | The zone where soil and rock are completely saturated |
| **Water table** | The transition between the zone of aeration and the zone of saturation |
| **Aquifer** | A subsurface layer of permeable rock or unconsolidated material — silt, sand, or gravel — through which groundwater can flow in amounts adequate for wells and springs |
| **Aquiclude** | The impermeable layer of rock below the groundwater |
| **Unconfined aquifer** | An aquifer with a permeable layer above and an impermeable layer below |
| **Confined aquifer** | An aquifer with impermeable layers both above and below |
| **Potentiometric surface** | The pressure level created by the pressure on the water in a confined aquifer — the level to which the water would rise if given the chance |
| **Ordinary well** | A well drilled into an unconfined aquifer; the water is not under pressure and must be pumped up |
| **Artesian well** | A well drilled into a confined aquifer; the water rises to the potentiometric surface |
| **Gushing artesian well** | An artesian well whose top is lower than the potentiometric surface, so the water rises out of the well on its own |
| **Drawdown** | The lowering of the water table of an unconfined aquifer, occurring when the rate of pumping exceeds the rate at which the aquifer can replenish itself |
| **Cone of depression** | The funnel-shaped dip in the lowered water table centred on a well |
| **Water withdrawal (non-consumptive use)** | The removal or diversion of water from surface or groundwater supplies followed by the return of that water to the same supply |
| **Consumptive use** | The permanent removal of water from the immediate environment; the water is not returned and is therefore not available for a second or third use |

# 4.1 Fluvial Processes and Channels

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Erosion and deposition

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Degradation** | Channel **erosion** |
| **Aggradation** | The channel **building up through deposition** — the opposite of degradation |

Every river is doing both somewhere along its length, and the balance between them determines the landforms in 4.2.

## Channel patterns

**Braided stream.** Excess sediment turns a stream into **interconnected channels**. This occurs when **reduced discharge lowers the stream's transporting ability**, or after a landslide delivers more sediment than the stream can carry. A braided pattern is therefore a sign that a stream is **overloaded**.

**Meandering stream.** Streams develop a more **sinuous** form. The tendency to meander is evidence of a river system's ability to find **the path of least effort** toward its base level — a river bends not at random but because bending distributes energy more evenly than a straight channel does.

## Anatomy of a meander

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **Undercut bank (cutbank)** | The place undergoing the **greatest erosive action** (scouring) — the **outside** of the bend, where flow is fastest |
| **Point bar** | Where **aggradation** occurs — accumulation of sediment on the **inside** of a meander bend, where flow is slowest |
| **Cutoff** | A narrow neck of land that is eventually eroded through |
| **Oxbow lake** | An **isolated meander**, left behind after a cutoff; debris and silt eventually fill it |
| **Meander scar** | Residual deposits marking previous river channels |

The cutbank and point bar are two halves of one process: because the fastest flow swings to the outside of a bend, meanders **erode outward and deposit inward**, which makes them migrate sideways across the floodplain over time. That migration eventually brings two bends close enough to cut through — producing an oxbow lake.

## The longitudinal profile

The **longitudinal profile** is the side view of a river from source to mouth.

A **graded stream** is one where the **channel slope has adjusted so that stream velocity is just enough to transport its sediment load** — neither eroding nor depositing overall. It is a state of equilibrium, and rivers tend toward it.

## Disturbing the equilibrium

**River rejuvenation** occurs when **tectonic uplift changes the elevation of a graded stream relative to its base level**. This **increases the stream gradient** and stimulates renewed erosion — a graded river thrown out of balance and forced to cut down again.

An **antecedent stream** is a rejuvenated river that **downcuts at the same rate as the tectonic uplift**, so it **maintains its course** even as a mountain range rises across it. The result is a river that appears to run straight through a mountain range, which it does — it was there first, and cut down as fast as the range went up.

A **nickpoint** (or knickpoint) is the point of interruption where the longitudinal profile contains an **abrupt change in gradient** — at a waterfall, for instance. Nickpoints migrate upstream as erosion works backward from them.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Degradation** | Channel erosion |
| **Aggradation** | The channel building up through deposition — the opposite of degradation |
| **Braided stream** | A stream turned into interconnected channels by excess sediment, occurring when reduced discharge lowers the stream's transporting ability or a landslide delivers more sediment than the stream can carry |
| **Meandering stream** | A stream that has developed a more sinuous form |
| **Undercut bank (cutbank)** | The place undergoing the greatest erosive action (scouring) — the outside of the bend, where flow is fastest |
| **Point bar** | Where aggradation occurs — accumulation of sediment on the inside of a meander bend, where flow is slowest |
| **Cutoff** | A narrow neck of land that is eventually eroded through |
| **Oxbow lake** | An isolated meander, left behind after a cutoff; debris and silt eventually fill it |
| **Meander scar** | Residual deposits marking previous river channels |
| **Longitudinal profile** | The side view of a river from source to mouth |
| **Graded stream** | A stream where the channel slope has adjusted so that stream velocity is just enough to transport its sediment load |
| **River rejuvenation** | What occurs when tectonic uplift changes the elevation of a graded stream relative to its base level, increasing the stream gradient and stimulating renewed erosion |
| **Antecedent stream** | A rejuvenated river that downcuts at the same rate as the tectonic uplift, so it maintains its course |
| **Nickpoint (knickpoint)** | The point of interruption where the longitudinal profile contains an abrupt change in gradient |

# 4.2 Fluvial Deposition and Landforms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Alluvium** is the general term for the unconsolidated **clay, silt, sand, gravel, and mineral fragments deposited by running water**. It may accumulate sorted or unsorted.

**Fluvial deposition** occurs when a stream deposits alluvium, creating depositional landforms — bars, floodplains, terraces, and deltas.

## Floodplain landforms

**Floodplain.** The flat, low-lying area adjacent to a channel and **subject to recurrent flooding**, layered with alluvial deposits that mask the underlying rock.

**Natural levees.** Low ridges of coarse sediment on either bank of some rivers. They form because when a river overtops its banks, the water immediately slows as it spreads out, so the **coarser, sand-sized particles are deposited first**, right along the bank, while finer material is carried further.

**Riparian marshes (backswamps).** Wetlands that form in the **poorly drained fine sediments** deposited by overbank flows — the finer material that the levees did not catch.

**Yazoo streams (yazoo tributaries).** Tributaries that **flow parallel to the main river but are blocked from joining it by the natural levees**, sometimes for many miles before finding a gap.

These three landforms are all consequences of a single event — a river overtopping its banks — sorted by grain size and drainage. The coarse fraction builds the levee, the fine fraction fills the backswamp, and the levee then traps the tributary.

**Alluvial terraces.** Produced by the **entrenchment of a river into its own floodplain** following tectonic uplift, they look like topographic **steps** above the river and generally appear in pairs on either side. They are the fossil record of river rejuvenation (4.1): each terrace is an abandoned floodplain from an earlier, higher stage.

## Arid-region landforms

**Alluvial fans.** In arid and semi-arid climates, prominent **cone- or fan-shaped deposits** of fluvial sediment, commonly at the **mouth of a canyon**. They form where a stream emerging from confined mountain terrain suddenly loses both its confinement and its gradient, dropping its load.

**Bajada.** Formed where individual alluvial fans **coalesce into one continuous sloping surface** along a mountain front.

**Playa.** The **salt crusts** left on the desert floor after water evaporates — the endpoint of drainage in a basin with no outlet.

## The river mouth

**Delta.** The level or nearly level **depositional plain that forms at the mouth of a river**, where the current slows on entering standing water and drops its sediment.

**Distributaries.** Channels running through the delta that **divide into smaller courses** — the opposite of tributaries, which combine.

**Estuary.** The body of water at a river's mouth **where freshwater flow encounters seawater**.

Whether a river builds a delta or an estuary depends on the balance between sediment supply and marine energy: a river delivering more sediment than tides and waves can remove builds a delta, while one delivering less is drowned into an estuary.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Alluvium** | The general term for the unconsolidated clay, silt, sand, gravel, and mineral fragments deposited by running water; it may accumulate sorted or unsorted |
| **Fluvial deposition** | When a stream deposits alluvium, creating depositional landforms — bars, floodplains, terraces, and deltas |
| **Floodplain** | The flat, low-lying area adjacent to a channel and subject to recurrent flooding, layered with alluvial deposits that mask the underlying rock |
| **Natural levees** | Low ridges of coarse sediment on either bank of some rivers, formed as an overtopping river slows and deposits its coarser, sand-sized particles first |
| **Riparian marshes (backswamps)** | Wetlands that form in the poorly drained fine sediments deposited by overbank flows |
| **Yazoo streams (yazoo tributaries)** | Tributaries that flow parallel to the main river but are blocked from joining it by the natural levees |
| **Alluvial terraces** | Topographic steps above a river, produced by the entrenchment of a river into its own floodplain following tectonic uplift; they generally appear in pairs on either side |
| **Alluvial fans** | In arid and semi-arid climates, prominent cone- or fan-shaped deposits of fluvial sediment, commonly at the mouth of a canyon |
| **Bajada** | The continuous sloping surface formed where individual alluvial fans coalesce along a mountain front |
| **Playa** | The salt crusts left on the desert floor after water evaporates |
| **Delta** | The level or nearly level depositional plain that forms at the mouth of a river |
| **Distributaries** | Channels running through the delta that divide into smaller courses |
| **Estuary** | The body of water at a river's mouth where freshwater flow encounters seawater |

# 5.1 Coastal Systems: Waves and Tides

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Forces driving coastal systems

**Internal forces:**

- **Tectonic movement**
- **Volcanic eruption and earthquake**
- **Vegetation stabilisation** — mangroves, salt marshes, and dune grasses trapping sediment
- Wide, low-gradient shorelines

**External forces:**

- **Atmospheric** — wind, climate
- **Ocean** — waves, storms, tides, eustatic sea-level rise, currents
- **Gravitational attraction** — moon, Earth, and Sun, producing tides
- **Land** — rivers delivering sediment

## Wave energy

**Wave energy** is transported through water — **the water itself does not travel with the wave**. This is the central idea of the topic, and everything about breaking waves follows from it.

- **Waves of transition** — the simple cyclic (orbital) motions water moves in as a wave passes
- **Waves of translation** — when **both energy and water** move toward the shore, which is what happens after a wave breaks

**Wave trains** are the groups in which waves travel. **Interference** describes how waves affect one another: **if waves are in phase, height is amplified; if not, they weaken** — the same superposition principle as in physics.

## Types of waves

**Wind waves.** Generated by winds in a stormy area of open ocean, known as the **fetch area**. Wave height depends on **wind velocity, duration, and fetch length**. Kinetic and potential energy increase within the fetch area.

**Swell waves.** Waves that have travelled **outside the fetch area** and are no longer driven by wind, but keep moving through **inertia**. They become **smooth, rounded, and long-crested** — which is why distant storms produce clean surf on calm days.

**Tsunami.** Triggered by **sudden, sharp motions of the seafloor** — earthquakes, landslides, volcanic activity. They are **hard to detect or forecast**, standing only **3 inches to 1 metre tall in the open sea** while their **wavelength can exceed 100 km**, and travelling at **600–800 km/h**. On approaching shore they become **much taller and much shorter in wavelength**.

That combination is what makes tsunamis so dangerous: at sea a ship may not notice one passing beneath it, because the enormous energy is spread over a wavelength of a hundred kilometres. In shallow water that same energy is compressed into a fraction of the distance, and it goes upward.

## Wave base and water depth

The **wave base** is the depth below which a wave no longer interacts with the seafloor, at **d = L/2** where **L** is wavelength.

| Category | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Deep water waves** | $d \ge L/2$ |
| **Transitional water waves** | $L/20 < d < L/2$ |
| **Shallow water waves** | $d \le L/20$ |

In general, waves curl over and break when either **$d \le 1.3h$** (depth approaches 1.3 times wave height) or the **steepness $H/L$** becomes too great.

## Types of breakers

| Breaker | Seafloor | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Spilling** | Flat or gentle | Waves steepen until the crest becomes unstable, producing **whitewater foam**; energy dissipates **slowly** |
| **Plunging** | Steeper, or a sudden depth change such as a sandbar | The crest becomes **vertical, curls over**, and drops onto the trough; releases most energy **at once** |
| **Surging** | Very steep beach with low-steepness waves | The crest **remains relatively unbroken** and slides up the beach; the wave base moves rapidly |

The gradient of the seafloor determines the type, and the type determines the erosional force delivered. A plunging breaker concentrates its whole energy at one point, which is why steep shores erode dramatically and gentle ones do not.

**Rip current.** When backwash from breakers flows back into the ocean in a **concentrated column**.

**Constructive waves** deposit more sediment than they erode, with a stronger swash than backwash. **Destructive waves** do the reverse.

## Tides

**Tides** are twice-daily oscillations in sea level.

**Tidal bulges** are the stretching of the fluid ocean caused by the **moon's gravitational pull** — and, on the opposite side of the Earth, by inertia, which is why there are two bulges and therefore two high tides a day.

- **Flood tide** — the incoming, high tide
- **Ebb tide** — the outgoing, low tide

| | Alignment | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Spring tide** | Sun and moon on the **same side** of Earth (or directly opposite) | **Highest** high tides and lowest lows — the pulls reinforce |
| **Neap tide** | Sun and moon at **right angles** | **Low high tides and high low tides** — the pulls partly cancel |

Spring tides have nothing to do with the season; the name refers to the water "springing" up.

## Zones of the coast

| Grouping | Zones |
|---|---|
| **Zones of wave influence** | Breaker zone, surf zone, swash zone (≈ foreshore) |
| **Zones of tide influence** | Backshore, foreshore, nearshore |
| **The sediment profile** | Berms, beach face, longshore bar |

## Sea level change

Factors that change sea level include tidal and wave processes in the short term, and **long-term changes in global temperature** in the long term — through both the melting of land ice and the thermal expansion of seawater.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Wave energy** | Energy transported through water — the water itself does not travel with the wave |
| **Waves of transition** | The simple cyclic (orbital) motions water moves in as a wave passes |
| **Waves of translation** | When both energy and water move toward the shore, which is what happens after a wave breaks |
| **Wave trains** | The groups in which waves travel |
| **Interference** | How waves affect one another: if waves are in phase, height is amplified; if not, they weaken |
| **Wind waves** | Waves generated by winds in a stormy area of open ocean; wave height depends on wind velocity, duration, and fetch length |
| **Fetch area** | The stormy area of open ocean in which wind waves are generated |
| **Swell waves** | Waves that have travelled outside the fetch area and are no longer driven by wind, but keep moving through inertia; they become smooth, rounded, and long-crested |
| **Tsunami** | A wave triggered by sudden, sharp motions of the seafloor — earthquakes, landslides, volcanic activity; 3 inches to 1 metre tall in the open sea with a wavelength that can exceed 100 km, travelling at 600–800 km/h, and becoming much taller and much shorter in wavelength on approaching shore |
| **Wave base** | The depth below which a wave no longer interacts with the seafloor, at $d = L/2$ where $L$ is wavelength |
| **Deep water waves** | Waves where $d \ge L/2$ |
| **Transitional water waves** | Waves where $L/20 < d < L/2$ |
| **Shallow water waves** | Waves where $d \le L/20$ |
| **Spilling breaker** | Over a flat or gentle seafloor, waves steepen until the crest becomes unstable, producing whitewater foam; energy dissipates slowly |
| **Plunging breaker** | Over a steeper seafloor or a sudden depth change such as a sandbar, the crest becomes vertical, curls over, and drops onto the trough; releases most energy at once |
| **Surging breaker** | On a very steep beach with low-steepness waves, the crest remains relatively unbroken and slides up the beach; the wave base moves rapidly |
| **Rip current** | When backwash from breakers flows back into the ocean in a concentrated column |
| **Constructive waves** | Waves that deposit more sediment than they erode, with a stronger swash than backwash |
| **Destructive waves** | Waves that erode more sediment than they deposit, with a stronger backwash than swash |
| **Tides** | Twice-daily oscillations in sea level |
| **Tidal bulges** | The stretching of the fluid ocean caused by the moon's gravitational pull, and on the opposite side of the Earth by inertia |
| **Flood tide** | The incoming, high tide |
| **Ebb tide** | The outgoing, low tide |
| **Spring tide** | With Sun and moon on the same side of Earth (or directly opposite), the pulls reinforce, giving the highest high tides and lowest lows |
| **Neap tide** | With Sun and moon at right angles, the pulls partly cancel, giving low high tides and high low tides |

# 5.2 Coastal Landforms and Coral Reefs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Erosional landforms

| Landform | Formation |
|---|---|
| **Sea arch** | An arch cut through a headland by erosion |
| **Sea stack** | Formed when an arch **collapses**, leaving an isolated tower in the water |
| **Wave-cut platform (wave-cut terrace)** | A **horizontal bench** cut by wave action in the tidal zone, extending from the foot of a sea cliff out into the sea |

Arches and stacks are stages of one sequence: waves exploit a weakness in a headland, open a cave, cut through to form an arch, and eventually the arch roof falls, leaving a stack. Finding a stack tells you an arch was there.

## Depositional landforms

| Landform | Formation |
|---|---|
| **Barrier spit** | Material deposited in a **long ridge extending out from a coast**, sometimes partially crossing and blocking a bay mouth |
| **Bay barrier (baymouth bar)** | When a spit **completely cuts off** a bay from the ocean |
| **Lagoon** | The shallow saltwater body left **cut off from the ocean** behind a bar |
| **Tombolo** | Where sediment deposits **connect the shoreline to an offshore island or sea stack** |

These are all products of **longshore drift** — the zigzag transport of sediment along a coast by waves arriving at an angle. A spit forms where the coastline turns but the drift continues in a straight line; extend it far enough and it becomes a baymouth bar with a lagoon behind it.

## Beach protection

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Breakwater** | Traps sand; built **parallel to the shore** |
| **Jetty** | Protects a river entrance to the sea **from deposition** |
| **Groin** | Traps sand — producing **deposition on one side and erosion on the other** |

The groin illustrates the central problem with coastal engineering. Interrupting longshore drift accumulates sand where you want it and starves the coast **downdrift**, which then erodes — so the neighbour builds a groin, and the problem moves along the coast. Coastal defences do not create sediment; they redistribute it.

## Coral reefs

Corals require narrow conditions, which is why reefs are geographically restricted:

| Requirement | Range |
|---|---|
| **Latitude** | Roughly 30°N to 30°S |
| **Temperature** | 18 °C – 29 °C |
| **Depth** | 10 – 55 m |
| **Salinity** | 27‰ – 40‰ |
| **Water clarity** | Clear and transparent, with little or no sedimentation |
| **Water motion** | Vigorous |

The depth and clarity requirements have the same cause: reef-building corals depend on symbiotic algae that need sunlight, so anything that blocks light — depth, sediment, turbidity — kills the reef. This is why coastal development and river sediment are as dangerous to reefs as temperature is.

### Three types of reef

**Fringing reefs** grow **seaward directly from the shore**, forming borders along shorelines and around islands.

**Barrier reefs** also border a shoreline, but instead of growing directly out from it they are **separated from land by a lagoon**.

**Atolls** are **ring-shaped** reefs, with a coral rim encircling a lagoon.

The three form a sequence around a subsiding volcanic island: a fringing reef grows on the new island's shore; as the island subsides the reef keeps growing upward and a lagoon opens between it and the shrinking land, making it a barrier reef; and when the island disappears entirely the ring of coral remains as an atoll. The reef records the island that used to be there.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sea arch** | An arch cut through a headland by erosion |
| **Sea stack** | An isolated tower in the water, formed when an arch collapses |
| **Wave-cut platform (wave-cut terrace)** | A horizontal bench cut by wave action in the tidal zone, extending from the foot of a sea cliff out into the sea |
| **Barrier spit** | Material deposited in a long ridge extending out from a coast, sometimes partially crossing and blocking a bay mouth |
| **Bay barrier (baymouth bar)** | A spit that completely cuts off a bay from the ocean |
| **Lagoon** | The shallow saltwater body left cut off from the ocean behind a bar |
| **Tombolo** | Where sediment deposits connect the shoreline to an offshore island or sea stack |
| **Longshore drift** | The zigzag transport of sediment along a coast by waves arriving at an angle |
| **Breakwater** | A structure built parallel to the shore to trap sand |
| **Jetty** | A structure protecting a river entrance to the sea from deposition |
| **Groin** | A structure that traps sand, producing deposition on one side and erosion on the other |
| **Fringing reef** | A reef growing seaward directly from the shore, forming borders along shorelines and around islands |
| **Barrier reef** | A reef bordering a shoreline but separated from land by a lagoon |
| **Atoll** | A ring-shaped reef, with a coral rim encircling a lagoon |

# 1.1 Plate Tectonics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Tectonic plates

The major tectonic plates are the **Eurasian, North American, South American, African, Antarctic, Indo-Australian, and Pacific**.

Plates move at about **2–10 cm per year**.

## Types of plate boundary

### 1. Divergent boundaries

Plates **move apart, creating new crust**.

### 2. Convergent boundaries

Plates collide, and what happens depends on which kinds of crust meet:

| Collision | Result |
|---|---|
| **Continent–continent** | **Forms mountains** |
| **Continent–ocean** | The **denser oceanic plate subducts** beneath the continental plate, forming **volcanic arcs** |
| **Ocean–ocean** | One oceanic plate subducts, creating **volcanic island arcs** |

Density is what decides: oceanic crust is denser, so it is the plate that goes under. When two continental plates meet, neither subducts, and the crust has nowhere to go but up.

### 3. Transform boundaries

Plates **slide past each other horizontally**.

## Folding and faulting

**Folding** — rocks **bend** under compressional forces, creating folds and, eventually, **metamorphic rocks** under pressure.

**Faulting** — rocks **break** under tension or compression, forming **faults** where blocks of crust move relative to each other.

Both are responses to the same forces; the difference is whether the rock deforms or fractures.

## Hot spots

**Hot spots** are areas where **magma rises through weakened portions of crust, forming volcanic islands**.

They are **located within tectonic plates** rather than at their boundaries, and are **caused by rising magma from the mantle** — which is why a volcano can appear far from any plate edge.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Divergent boundary** | A boundary where plates move apart, creating new crust |
| **Convergent boundary** | A boundary where plates collide: continent–continent forms mountains; continent–ocean subducts the denser oceanic plate, forming volcanic arcs; ocean–ocean subducts one plate, creating volcanic island arcs |
| **Transform boundary** | A boundary where plates slide past each other horizontally |
| **Folding** | Rocks bending under compressional forces, creating folds and, eventually, metamorphic rocks under pressure |
| **Faulting** | Rocks breaking under tension or compression, forming faults where blocks of crust move relative to each other |
| **Hot spots** | Areas where magma rises through weakened portions of crust, forming volcanic islands; located within tectonic plates and caused by rising magma from the mantle |

# 2.1 Volcanoes and Natural Disasters

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Natural disasters

A **natural disaster** is defined as **the impact of natural hazards that cause significant human, financial, or environmental loss**.

The definition turns on **impact**. The hazard is the eruption or the earthquake; the disaster is the loss it causes.

## Volcanoes

A **volcano** is a **mountain or hill with a vent that releases lava, steam, and ash**.

### How volcanoes form

Volcanoes occur at **divergent boundaries, convergent boundaries, and hot spots**:

- **Divergent** — found at plate boundaries where **plates pull apart**
- **Convergent** — occur where **plates collide, causing subduction**
- **Hot spots** — **located within tectonic plates**, caused by **rising magma from the mantle**

## Types of volcano

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Cinder cone** | Small, **steep-sided** cones made of pyroclastic material; found near fault lines and subduction zones |
| **Shield** | Large, **gently sloping** domes formed by **mafic lava** |
| **Composite** | Tall, cone-shaped, with **steep slopes**; layers of lava and ash; the **most dangerous type** |
| **Caldera** | Large volcanic craters formed **after massive eruptions** |

## Lava types

- **Mafic lava** — **low viscosity**
- **Felsic lava** — high viscosity

Viscosity is what links lava to volcano shape. Low-viscosity mafic lava flows freely and spreads into the broad, gentle slopes of a shield volcano; thicker felsic lava cannot flow far and builds the steep cones described above.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Natural disaster** | The impact of natural hazards that cause significant human, financial, or environmental loss |
| **Volcano** | A mountain or hill with a vent that releases lava, steam, and ash |
| **Hot spots** | Volcanic sites located within tectonic plates, caused by rising magma from the mantle |
| **Cinder cone** | A small, steep-sided cone made of pyroclastic material; found near fault lines and subduction zones |
| **Shield** | A large, gently sloping dome formed by mafic lava |
| **Composite** | A tall, cone-shaped volcano with steep slopes and layers of lava and ash; the most dangerous type |
| **Caldera** | A large volcanic crater formed after a massive eruption |
| **Mafic lava** | Lava of low viscosity |
| **Felsic lava** | Lava of high viscosity |
